title: Fly agaric (Amanita muscaria)
summary: The red mushroom with white warts. What you see is only the fruit of a much larger fungus whose threads run through the soil and partner with the roots of trees.

layers.basics: The fly agaric is a toadstool: a red cap dotted with white warts on a white stem, with a ring on the stem and a swollen base. It is poisonous and can put people, especially children, and pets in hospital: never eat a wild mushroom on the strength of an app or a photograph. The mushroom is not the whole organism. It is the short-lived fruit body that a fungus builds above ground to release spores, the way an apple tree makes apples. The rest of the fungus is a web of fine threads in the soil, and it swaps minerals and water for sugar with the roots of nearby trees. Use the layer buttons: cut it in half, look underground, or follow how it grows from a small white egg.
layers.deeper: Fungi are not plants. They have no chlorophyll and cannot make their own food; they absorb it. Their cell walls are made of chitin (the same material as insect shells), and genetically they are closer kin to animals than to plants. This species feeds in partnership: its threads wrap the finest roots of trees (an ectomycorrhiza) and exchange materials with them. Each fruit body goes through three visible stages: a button wrapped in a white veil, a half-open cap with the veil tearing, and a mature flat cap. The white warts and the ring are what is left of two veils that once enclosed the young mushroom.
layers.expert: Amanita muscaria is a basidiomycete (Agaricales), a mushroom that makes its spores on gill surfaces, four to a spore-making cell (basidium). The fruit body is a small part of the fungal individual; the fruit bodies in one patch may or may not come from the same mycelium. It contains ibotenic acid and muscimol, which act on glutamate and GABA receptors in the nervous system. It is native to temperate and boreal woodland across the northern hemisphere and has been carried to the southern hemisphere with planted trees. The park model is a reconstruction from typical measurements; sizes, counts and layer thicknesses that the model chooses are said so on the cards.

facts: ≈ 9–13 × 6.5–9 µm, white in a spore print
ibotenic acid and muscimol: poisonings often need medical care; deaths are very rare; other Amanita species can be deadly
pine, spruce, fir and birch are commonly reported; the list varies by region
open_questions: How the many fly agaric lineages around the world relate to each other, and how much of the species counts as one species, is still being worked out.

title: Cap (pileus)
summary: The cap is the umbrella-shaped top of the fruit body: a red skin over white flesh, with the spore-making gills on its underside.

layers.basics: The cap is bright red, sometimes orange or yellowish, and dotted with white warts. It starts as a ball, becomes a dome, and ends nearly flat as the mushroom opens. Its job is to hold the gills up and out in the air so that spores can fall away. A mature cap in the park is 14 cm across, a typical size; the species ranges from about 5 to 30 cm.
layers.deeper: From the top down the cap is a thin red skin (the cuticle), a thin yellowish layer under it, and thick white flesh made of tightly packed fungal threads. Underneath hang the gills. The warts are not part of the skin: they are fragments of the veil that once wrapped the whole young mushroom, and they become less obvious as the cap widens and as rain washes them off.
layers.expert: Red varieties are var. muscaria; other forms are yellow to orange (var. guessowii in north-eastern North America) or have yellow warts. The warts keep their size while the cap grows, so they spread apart as the cap expands. The model cap uses a chosen profile (convex, slightly dished underneath) and 150 warts of chosen sizes. The park model is a reconstruction from typical measurements; sizes, counts and layer thicknesses that the model chooses are said so on the cards.

facts: ball, then dome, then nearly flat
bright red; orange or yellow forms exist

title: Cuticle: the red skin
summary: The skin of the cap is a thin red layer; just under it is a yellowish layer. Together they are far thinner than they look in the cut model.

layers.basics: The bright red skin is the cap's surface layer. If you cut a cap, you find a thin yellow layer just beneath the red, and below that, white flesh.
layers.deeper: In the cut-open model the red and yellow bands are drawn about a millimetre or two thick so that you can see them; the real skin is thinner. A yellowish layer is also seen under the veil of a young specimen when it is dissected.
layers.expert: Cap colour varies between forms of the species, from red to orange to yellow, and the red cap of the common form fades towards reddish orange in sunlight.

facts: red cuticle, yellow layer, white flesh
drawn thick to be visible (not measured)

ext.title: Duffy: Amanita muscaria and A. pantherina, Toxic Fungi of Western North America (MykoWeb)

title: Cap flesh: a tissue made of threads
summary: The white flesh of the cap is a packed mass of fungal threads called hyphae, each one a chain of cells.

layers.basics: Cut a cap and the white flesh looks solid. Under a microscope it is a tangle of very thin tubes, each a few thousandths of a millimetre wide, packed together. Each tube is a hypha, a chain of cells divided by cross-walls. The whole mushroom, like all the rest of the fungus, is built from these threads.
layers.deeper: Hyphae are typically 2 to 10 micrometres across and grow at their tips. Their walls are made of chitin and glucans. In the flesh the hyphae are interwoven and pressed together; in the soil the same kind of thread runs loosely as the mycelium. Click a thread in the tissue scene to see chitin's building block.
layers.expert: The tissue scene draws threads about 6 µm wide, inside the usual range; their number, direction and layout are illustrative. Real mushroom flesh also contains other cell shapes, such as swollen cells among the threads, which the scene does not show.

title: Hypha: the fungal thread
summary: A hypha is one thread of a fungus: a long, thin tube that grows from its tip and has a wall of chitin.

layers.basics: Fungi grow as threads. A hypha lengthens at its tip, branches, and joins with others. It is a tube about 2 to 10 micrometres wide. Fungi feed by releasing digestive enzymes into their surroundings and absorbing what dissolves, and the huge surface area of a web of hyphae makes that efficient.
layers.deeper: The tube is walled with chitin (a chain of N-acetylglucosamine units) woven with glucans. Chitin is also what insect shells are made of. Plant walls are made of cellulose instead.
layers.expert: The tissue scene lets you reach the chitin building block (N-acetylglucosamine, `n_acetylglucosamine` in the molecule set) from any thread.

title: Warts: remnants of the universal veil
summary: The white warts are pieces of a veil that once wrapped the whole young mushroom. They are not part of the cap itself.

layers.basics: When a fly agaric is a small white egg, it is wrapped in a skin called the universal veil. As the mushroom grows, the veil stretches and breaks. Bits of it stay on the cap as white or yellowish warts, and bits stay at the base. Rain and age can wash the warts off, so an old cap can be nearly bare.
layers.deeper: The warts are small pyramid-shaped patches. They do not grow with the cap, so on a young cap they sit close together and on an old cap they are far apart. Other Amanita species have warts too, which is why wart patterns are not enough to identify a mushroom.
layers.expert: The model places 150 warts of chosen size on the mature cap and the same layout on the half-open one, which is why they are denser there. A real cap's count varies. Wart colour in the species is white to yellow.

facts: keep their size; less prominent as the cap expands; wash off

title: Gills (lamellae)
summary: Gills are the thin vertical plates under the cap. Their surface is covered by the cells that make spores.

layers.basics: Look under a mature cap and you see dozens of thin white plates fanned out from the stem to the rim. These are the gills. Each plate is lined on both sides with tiny spore-making cells. Packing many thin plates under a cap gives far more surface for spores than a smooth underside would. Fly agaric gills are white and do not touch the stem: there is a small gap, which is what "free" means.
layers.deeper: The plates are not all the same length. Long gills run from near the stem to the rim, and shorter ones lie between them near the rim. The model uses 56 long gills, 56 of two-thirds length and 112 of two-fifths length (224 in all, a chosen count).
layers.expert: The gill count is the model's; real counts vary. Spore colour in a deposit (spore print) is white in this species. The gill plates are drawn about half a millimetre thick, a chosen value.

title: Inside a gill: the spore-making layer (hymenium)
summary: A gill is a thin sheet of threads with a skin of spore-making cells on each face. Each of these cells, a basidium, makes four spores.

layers.basics: Cut across a gill and you see three parts. In the middle is a thin core of loose threads that holds the gill up. On each side is a layer of small supporting cells, and on the outside a crowded layer of club-shaped cells called basidia. This outer layer is the hymenium. Each basidium puts out four tiny prongs, and a spore grows on the tip of each.
layers.deeper: A basidium usually carries four spores, though two or eight happen in other species. When a spore is ripe, a drop of water forms at its tip and another on its side. When the two drops merge, the sudden change in surface tension launches the spore. In gilled mushrooms the spore travels less than 0.1 mm, just clear of the gill, and then falls down between the plates and out from under the cap into the air.
layers.expert: In the tissue scene the spore length (about 11 µm; the species range is 9–13 × 6.5–9 µm) and thread width are true to the sources; the size of the basidia and the thickness of the gill layers are illustrative, and a real gill carries enormous numbers of basidia. The arrangement of threads in the gill's core is simplified.

facts: surface-tension catapult; < 0.1 mm travel in gilled mushrooms

ext.title: Stolze-Rybczynski et al. 2009: Adaptation of the spore discharge mechanism in the Basidiomycota (PLoS ONE)

title: Spores: how many and how far
summary: A mushroom releases an enormous number of spores. Each is a single cell with a tough wall that can ride the air to new places.

layers.basics: A spore is the fungus's seed-like unit: one cell, much smaller than a seed, that can grow into a new network of threads if it lands somewhere good. The fly agaric's spores are white, oval and about 11 micrometres long. Most land and die; a few find the right soil and a root. A single mushroom sheds a very large number of spores, and how many depends on its size, age and the weather.
layers.deeper: Spores are carried out from under the cap by air movement after the launch from the gill. The figure shown here is the size of one spore, the one measurement of this species that the card states.
layers.expert: Spores are the haploid products of meiosis in the basidium; two compatible threads grown from different spores must fuse for the mushroom stage to form.

ext.title: Stolze-Rybczynski et al. 2009: Adaptation of the spore discharge mechanism in the Basidiomycota (PLoS ONE)

title: Stipe (stem)
summary: The stem lifts the cap into the air so that spores can fall clear and be carried by the wind.

layers.basics: The white stem holds the cap high above the ground. In a mature fly agaric it is 5 to 20 cm tall and 1 to 2 cm wide, smooth above the ring and fibrous to scaly below it. It widens into a swollen base at the soil. Inside, it is made of threads like those of the cap.
layers.deeper: The ring partway up and the scales at the base are leftovers of the veils.
layers.expert: The model's stem is 14 cm tall (chosen in the range 5–20 cm), 1.7 cm wide under the cap (range 1–2 cm), with a swollen base 4 cm wide (chosen). The model draws the stem as one solid piece; the inside of a real stem varies.

title: Ring (annulus) and partial veil
summary: The ring is a skirt of thin white tissue on the stem: what is left of a second veil that covered the gills of the young mushroom.

layers.basics: A young mushroom has a second protective sheet, the partial veil, stretched from the rim of the cap to the stem. It covers the gills while the spores ripen. When the cap opens, the sheet tears away from the rim and hangs on the stem as a ring. With age it often droops and goes floppy. In the half-open specimen in the park you can see the veil still joined to the cap rim.
layers.deeper: The universal veil wrapped the whole button; the partial veil is a separate, inner layer that protects only the gills. This difference is why a fly agaric has two kinds of leftover: warts and base scales from the first, the ring from the second.
layers.expert: The ring is white and can be wide. The model draws a scalloped skirt with a chosen radius of 3.4 cm and thickness; the scalloping is a stylistic choice, as the real rim varies.

title: Swollen base and the volva
summary: The base of the stem is swollen, and its surface carries rings of scales: the remains of the lower part of the first veil.

layers.basics: At the soil, the stem swells into a bulb. When the young mushroom pushed out of its white egg, the lower part of the egg's skin broke and stayed behind. On a fly agaric it stays attached as a few rings of scales around the bulb rather than a cup. This is a good clue when identifying Amanita mushrooms, because some of them have a cup (volva) at the base.
layers.deeper: The species account describes the bulb as having universal veil remnants in the form of two to four distinct rings or ruffs. The model draws three rings of small scales on the bulb, a chosen count.
layers.expert: The scales are drawn as small recurved flakes; their real shape and size vary.

facts: Rings or ruffs on the bulb

title: Button (egg) stage
summary: The young fly agaric emerges as a white egg-shaped lump. Inside, the cap, gills and stem are already formed, tiny and folded.

layers.basics: The first sign of a mushroom is a tiny knob in the soil. It grows into a white egg-shaped button wrapped in the universal veil. If you cut a button in half, there is a small red cap pressed against a short stem, with the young gills in a chamber below, and a thick white veil around it all. The cut button in the park is drawn from this description.
layers.deeper: The very first stage, the primordium, is a nodule under 2 mm across; it expands into the button. Dissecting a young specimen shows a yellowish layer of skin under the veil. The thickness of the veil in the cut model is a chosen 2.6 mm; real veils vary.
layers.expert: The button in the park is 4.7 cm tall (chosen). The inner arrangement drawn in the cut view is schematic: the proportions come from the model, not a section of a real button.

title: Half-open stage: the veil tears
summary: In the middle stage the cap is a dome and the veils are splitting; the gills are still hidden behind the partial veil.

layers.basics: As the stem lengthens and the cap swells, the white egg skin splits and slips down, leaving warts on the cap. The cap is still a dome, folded down around the stem, and the partial veil still hides the gills. Later the cap flattens, the veil tears from its rim, and the gills are open to the air.
layers.deeper: In the park, three separate fruit bodies stand side by side to show the sequence; they are not one mushroom over time. The half-open one has the same 150 warts as the mature one on a smaller cap, which is why they are closer together.
layers.expert: The model does not show the timing from button to open cap. The proportions of the half-open specimen are a chosen interpolation between the button and the mature cap.

facts: present; denser than on the mature cap

title: A fly agaric cut in half
summary: Cut in half, the mushroom shows a thin red skin, white flesh, gills hanging free of the stem, and a white stem with a ring and a swollen base.

layers.basics: Slice a fly agaric from top to bottom and you see its layers at once: the thin red skin of the cap, a yellowish layer under it, thick white flesh, and the gills hanging in the space below the cap. The stem runs straight up the middle and swells at the base. The ring is a thin skirt that sticks out from the stem. Click a part of the cut surface, or a yellow marker.
layers.deeper: This is a model cut, not a photograph. The gill in the cutting plane is drawn lengthwise; the other gills in the kept half are drawn behind it. The bands of skin are drawn a millimetre or so thick to be visible. The button beside it is cut the same way, to show the young structures inside its veil.
layers.expert: Cut-open views in this park are reconstructions from the proportions chosen for the model. A real cut mushroom shows more variation (insect tunnels, moisture, discolouring).

facts: red skin, yellow layer, white flesh

title: Mycelium: the hidden fungus
summary: Under the mushroom is the fungus itself: a spreading web of fine threads that may be much larger than the mushroom and last much longer.

layers.basics: The mushroom is only the fruit. The fungus is the web of threads (the mycelium) in the soil, which absorbs water and nutrients and reaches the roots of trees. A mycelium can be far bigger than the mushroom it produces. In the underground view, the white lines are the web, drawn several hundred times too thick so that you can see them.
layers.deeper: Each thread is a hypha, 2 to 10 micrometres across; hyphae can bunch into thicker cords, which let a mycelium move water and nutrients over distance. Some are drawn here as cords linking the three fruit bodies to a hub and spreading outwards; some run to the root tips of the host tree. The layout is a drawing of the idea, not a map of a real mycelium.
layers.expert: The thinnest threads drawn are about 2 mm wide against a real width of about 5 µm: several hundred times too thick. One honey fungus (Armillaria ostoyae), a parasite that also feeds on dead wood, covers about 9 km² (2,385 acres) of forest in Oregon, which shows how large a single mycelium can become.

facts: ≈ 2–4.5 mm, several hundred times too thick

ext.title: Oregon Encyclopedia: Humongous fungus, Armillaria ostoyae

title: Root of a partner tree
summary: The fly agaric forms a partnership with the roots of certain trees. The root shown stands for a pine or birch, which are well-documented partners.

layers.basics: This fungus does not live alone. Its threads attach to the fine roots of living trees and swap goods with them. Pine, spruce, fir and birch are among the trees it is commonly reported with, and where it has been carried to the southern hemisphere it grows with planted pines and under southern beech (Nothofagus). The root in the underground view is a generic root of such a tree; the tree itself is off the edge of the model.
layers.deeper: This fungus is a partner of living trees rather than a decomposer of dead wood, which is why it is found in woods and under trees. For the tree's side of such a partnership, see the oak's card on its mycorrhiza, which tells the story for a different tree.
layers.expert: Pine and birch are the best-documented partners. The set of trees a given fly agaric mycelium is joined to varies from region to region.

facts: a generic root; the tree is off the model

title: Mycorrhizal root tip (ectomycorrhiza)
summary: A mycorrhizal root tip is a tree's finest root wrapped in a sleeve of fungus, with fungal threads growing between its outer cells.

layers.basics: The very ends of the tree's finest roots do not look bare. Each is covered by a sheath of fungal threads, the mantle, and more threads reach outwards into the soil. Inside, the fungus grows between the root's outer cells (never into them), in a net where tree and fungus touch. The tips in the park are drawn much larger than life so you can see them.
layers.deeper: The sheath (mantle) is a layer of tightly woven threads whose thickness varies with the fungus and the tree. The inner net of threads between the root cells is the Hartig net. In this type of partnership, called ectomycorrhiza, the fungus never enters the root cells. About 2 per cent of plant species form it (Brundrett and Tedersoo 2018), mostly woody plants, and the fungi are mainly basidiomycetes and ascomycetes. Click the tissue scene to see mantle, net and cells.
layers.expert: In most flowering trees the net stays in the outermost layer of root cells, while in conifers such as pine it reaches deeper into the cortex. The tissue scene is schematic: real tips are rounded and branched, and the cells are not boxes.

facts: around the root and between cells, not inside them

ext.title: Brundrett and Tedersoo 2018: Evolutionary history of mycorrhizal symbioses and global host plant diversity (New Phytologist)

title: Mantle: the fungal sleeve
summary: The mantle is a layer of tightly woven fungal threads that covers the tip of the root.

layers.basics: The mantle is the outer part of the partnership: a sleeve of fungus around the root tip. It is dense, so that the root surface is covered. From its outside, the threads reach out into the soil and make up the mycelium.
layers.deeper: Mantle thickness varies with the fungus and the tree; in the tissue scene, the mantle is drawn as four rows of threads, a schematic choice. Threads in the soil can carry water to the mantle, and some cords carry it over larger distances.
layers.expert: The mantle sits between the soil and the root surface, so what the root takes up from the fungus and gives to it passes through or around this layer.

title: Hartig net: where tree and fungus meet
summary: The Hartig net is fungal threads that grow between the outer cells of the root: the surface where the swap happens.

layers.basics: Between the tree's root cells, the fungus pushes thin threads that wind around each cell like a net. These do not enter the cells: the fungus stays outside and touches the walls. The tree and the fungus pass materials across this shared surface.
layers.deeper: In conifers such as pine the net reaches deep into the root cortex; in most flowering trees it stays in the outermost cell layer (Brundrett, mycorrhizas.info). Either way the net greatly increases the contact surface between partners.
layers.expert: Which transporters carry sugars and nutrients across this interface is an active research area.

facts: between root cells, not inside them

title: The swap: sugar for minerals
summary: The tree gives the fungus sugar; the fungus gives the tree water and minerals such as nitrogen and phosphate. How much each side gains depends on the soil and the conditions.

layers.basics: A tree makes sugar in its leaves by photosynthesis, and it sends some of it down to its roots. The fungus cannot make sugar from sunlight, but it is far better than a root at gathering minerals and water from the soil, because its threads are so thin and so numerous. So the two exchange: the tree supplies sugar, and the fungus supplies nitrogen, phosphorus and water.
layers.deeper: The shares vary with site and method. In one arctic tundra study, mycorrhizal fungi were estimated to supply 61 to 86 per cent of the nitrogen in the plants, while the plants gave 8 to 17 per cent of their photosynthetic carbon to the fungi (Hobbie and Hobbie 2006). The same paper cites field estimates of 2.5 to 14 per cent of gross primary production going to ectomycorrhizal fungi and culture studies of 1 to 11 per cent. Phosphorus is handed over largely as phosphate ions. Tree sugar travels in the phloem as sucrose.
layers.expert: Whether trees share much carbon or chemical signals through fungal networks that connect several trees is disputed: Karst and colleagues (2023) judge the evidence for forest-wide sharing too sparse and unsettled. In culture the fly agaric grows on glucose or fructose but not on sucrose, so the sucrose a tree sends is first split into those two sugars by an enzyme at the root before the fungus takes it up (Nehls et al. 2000). The molecules in the tissue scene (sucrose for the tree's sugar, phosphate for the minerals) are named as the standard forms; the scene is schematic.

facts: Plant carbon given to fungi (one tundra study)
Plant nitrogen from fungi (one tundra study)
open_questions: Do trees share meaningful amounts of carbon and chemical signals through fungal networks that join them in real forests? The evidence is disputed and the question is open.

title: Ways of living: rot, partner or parasite
summary: Some fungi feed on dead material, some exchange materials with living trees, and some feed on living hosts. The fly agaric is a partner.

layers.basics: Many fungi are decomposers: they digest dead wood, leaves and dung, and return nutrients to the soil. Others, like the fly agaric, partner with living plants. The two lifestyles use the same kind of threads but have different needs: a decomposer needs dead food, while a partner needs a living tree and supplies it with minerals and water. A third group, the parasites, feed on living hosts.
layers.deeper: Fungi are described as the principal decomposers in ecosystems. Most land plants form a mycorrhiza: in a survey of vascular plant species, 72 per cent were arbuscular mycorrhizal, 2 per cent ectomycorrhizal, 1.5 per cent ericoid and 10 per cent orchid mycorrhizal, and only 8 per cent never form one (Brundrett and Tedersoo 2018). Fly agaric is a partner of living trees.
layers.expert: The line between the lifestyles is not sharp: honey fungi (Armillaria), for example, feed on living wood and go on feeding on it after the tree dies.

facts: Plant species that form a mycorrhiza
≈ 85 % (72 % arbuscular, 2 % ecto-, 1.5 % ericoid, 10 % orchid; Brundrett and Tedersoo 2018)

ext.title: Brundrett and Tedersoo 2018: Evolutionary history of mycorrhizal symbioses and global host plant diversity (New Phytologist)

title: Chitin: the fungal wall and our kinship
summary: Fungal walls are made of chitin, the same material as insect shells. Fungi are closer relatives of animals than of plants.

layers.basics: A mushroom looks like a plant that stands still, but it is not one. It cannot make its own food, it absorbs it. Its cell walls are made of chitin, which animals such as insects and crabs use for their hard shells, not the cellulose plants use. And when biologists compare genes, fungi turn out to be more closely related to animals than to plants.
layers.deeper: Chitin is a long chain of N-acetylglucosamine units. Fungal walls combine chitin with glucans. Fungi and animals belong to one major group of organisms (the opisthokonts) and plants to another; the dates of these splits are estimates from molecular clocks and fossils and remain uncertain.
layers.expert: The molecule appears in this app as N-acetylglucosamine (the repeating unit). You can reach it from any thread in the tissue scenes by pressing the molecule button.

facts: fungi are closer kin to animals than to plants (dates uncertain)

title: Ibotenic acid and muscimol
summary: The fly agaric contains two chemicals that act on the brain: ibotenic acid, which excites nerve cells, and muscimol, which dampens them. They make the mushroom poisonous.

layers.basics: These two substances are made by the mushroom and they disturb how nerve cells talk to each other. Ibotenic acid looks like the brain's main excitatory messenger (glutamate). Muscimol looks like the brain's main calming messenger (GABA). In a person who eats the mushroom, the result can be confusion, nausea, twitching, hallucinations and, in severe cases, seizures or coma. This is poisoning, not a treat: never eat a wild mushroom on the strength of an app or a photograph.
layers.deeper: Ibotenic acid is a close chemical relative of muscimol and is partly converted to it in the body. Muscimol is a potent agonist of GABA type A receptors: it opens chloride channels and quiets neurons. Ibotenic acid acts like glutamate at NMDA receptors. Muscimol is C4H6N2O2, molar mass about 114 g/mol. Muscarine, the substance the species is named after, is present at levels too low to explain the poisoning, and the deadly amatoxins of some other Amanita species are not present.
layers.expert: Two molecules are missing from this app's molecule set: ibotenic acid and muscimol; their shape is not shown. GABA, which muscimol imitates, is present and is linked here. The amount of toxin varies strongly with season and place.

facts: Amatoxins (the deadly toxins of some other Amanita species)
not present in the fly agaric
open_questions: The amounts of ibotenic acid and muscimol vary widely between mushrooms and between seasons, and the reasons are not well understood.

ext.title: INCHEM poisons information monograph: Amanita muscaria and A. pantherina

title: Poisoning: what is known, and what to do
summary: Fly agaric poisoning is real and often needs hospital care. Deaths are rare, but children and pets are at particular risk. Never eat a wild mushroom on the strength of an app.

layers.basics: Fly agaric poisoning happens: to small children who put things in their mouths, to people who mistake it for an edible mushroom, to people who eat it on purpose, and to dogs. Symptoms usually begin 30 to 90 minutes after eating and are strongest at about 2 to 3 hours. They can include nausea and vomiting, drowsiness, twitching, confusion and hallucination, and in severe cases seizures, trouble breathing or coma. Seizures are reported mainly in children. There is no antidote: doctors treat the symptoms and protect the airway, and some patients have needed a breathing machine for days. If someone, or a pet, may have eaten one, call a poison centre or emergency services at once. Never eat a wild mushroom on the strength of an app, a photograph or a description.
layers.deeper: Poison-information monographs describe deaths from these toxins as extremely rare, and attribute them to complications. That is not the same as harmless. In a review of 34 cases reported to one US regional poison centre in 2002 to 2016, none died, but five patients were intubated (Moss and Hendrickson 2019). In Minnesota in 2018 a man who ate fly agaric was intubated and ventilated for four days and left hospital after eight (CDC 2019). A fatal case in a dog, confirmed by DNA and chemical tests, has been published. Most poisonings happen when a mushroom is mistaken for an edible one. Other Amanita species look quite different and can be deadly: A. bisporigera, which contains amatoxins, caused an outbreak in Minnesota in 2006 that made nine people ill and killed one.
layers.expert: Doses and preparation are deliberately not given here or anywhere in this explorer. Clinical features come from a poison-information monograph and from case series; the numbers in them are small, so they describe what has been seen, not what will happen to any one person.

facts: none; treatment is supportive and may need hospital care
extremely rare (monograph); not zero for other Amanita species
